paragraphs.text: A loose [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, made in the 1980s. Raw pu’er is never given the fast fermentation that makes shou. Instead it [changes slowly in storage](sheng:aging), so the years this leaf has kept, and the places it was kept, are part of what it has become.

The trade does not agree on [when raw pu’er counts as aged](sheng:ageing). Some say ten years, and many wait for twenty or more. Made in the 1980s, this leaf is past both marks. It comes from the decade when [collectors of aged raw pu’er](sheng:history-modern), led at first by Taiwan, began looking for teas like it.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
